title: Moq
description: The most popular mocking library for .NET, using LINQ and lambda expressions.

data.text: `Moq` is the most widely used mocking library for .NET. It uses LINQ and lambda expressions to create, configure, and verify mocks without requiring any mock generation tools or runtime proxies.
Use `Mock<T>` to create a mock of an interface or class. Configure behavior with `Setup` and verify interactions with `Verify`.

data.title: Tip
data.text: Use `It.IsAny<T>()` and `It.Is<T>(predicate)` to match flexible arguments in mock setups and verifications.

Moq creates a test double from a `Mock<T>`. A stub returns a value with `Setup`, a mock is checked afterward with `Verify`, and `It.IsAny<T>()` matches any argument. The distinction between the two matters: a stub provides input to the code under test, a mock asserts an interaction the code should have produced.

data.title: Setting up returns and verifying a call
Interview angle: stub the query, verify the command
data.text: Overusing `Verify` couples a test to the exact sequence of calls, so a harmless refactor breaks it. The rule of thumb is to stub queries — what a dependency returns — and verify commands, the side effects the code under test is responsible for. Saying that shows you think about a test that survives refactoring.

data.title: Key Takeaways
points: Moq uses Mock<T> to create mocks
Setup configures return values and behaviors
It.IsAny<T>() matches any argument of type T
data.takeaway: Moq makes mocking in .NET tests concise and strongly typed.
